query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A targeted heat‐treatment that induces phase‐selective recrystallization of the soft (fcc) phase while retaining the hard (B2) framework in a eutectic high-entropy alloy will simultaneously enhance yield strength and ductility relative to the as-cast lamellar microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine dual-phase lamellar microstructure (e.g., fcc + B2)
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to a controlled thermo‐mechanical treatment (i.e. a carefully selected annealing step possibly following pre-deformation) that preferentially recrystallizes the fcc (soft) phase while preserving the structural integrity of the B2 (hard) phase.
generation.conditions: The treatment is performed under conditions chosen to promote phase-selective recrystallization (with annealing temperature and time optimized to fully recrystallize the fcc phase) and evaluated under room-temperature quasi‐static tensile loading; all other parameters (composition, casting route) remain unchanged.
generation.structural_mediator: A composite microstructure in which a fully recrystallized, ductile fcc phase is embedded within a continuous, intact hard B2 skeletal framework
generation.mechanism: Recrystallizing only the soft phase eliminates weak phase boundaries and enhances its strain hardening capacity, while the hard phase sustains overall strength; the improved strain partitioning delays crack initiation and propagation during deformation, thereby overcoming the typical strength–ductility trade-off.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast baseline, the treated alloy is expected to show an increase in both yield strength and tensile ductility (e.g., reaching uniform elongations similar to or exceeding ~35% and higher effective flow stress), though the precise magnitude requires experimental verification.
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a naturally formed fcc + B2 lamellar structure without any additional selective recrystallization treatment
generation.boundary: The intervention is applied while keeping the alloy composition, casting process, and testing regime unchanged; only the post-solidification heat treatment is modified.
generation.uncertainty: Exact annealing temperatures, durations, and pre-deformation conditions necessary to achieve ideal phase-selective recrystallization are not yet defined and must be optimized during experimental trials.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same as-cast eutectic HEA batch. One set receives the proposed phase-selective recrystallization treatment (optimized annealing/pre-deformation protocol), while the control set remains as-cast. Both sets are then subjected to room-temperature quasi-static tensile testing and detailed microstructural analysis (using EBSD/TEM) to assess phase characteristics.
measurements: Microstructural features (extent of recrystallization in the fcc phase and integrity of B2 phase)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show a statistically significant simultaneous increase in both strength and ductility compared to the as-cast control, or if the microstructural analysis does not confirm a selective recrystallization of the fcc phase without degrading the hard phase, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa. This concept is universal for various duplex alloys with soft and hard phases and opens new frontiers for traditional eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials.
